speechtext: When the leaders of both parties join to pay tribute to a deceased citizen I admire their eulogy, but when they pay such compliments to a man still among us I am a little suspicious. Mr. Marler is full of dignity; he is a very dignified diplomat; he is one of the most dignified diplomats in the world; he impresses everyone by his dignity. I do not see how he can increase our business in China and in the other countries of the far east, or solve the Indian problem, or keep the bolshevists under control. But he is always dignified: his smile is dignified; his gesture is dignified; his voice is sweet-and dignified; bis words are impressive-and dignified. But, Mr. Chairman, in joining my tribute to that which has been paid him by the leaders of both parties, may I express the fear that if the monarchical system is reestablished in China the Chinese may steal the hon. gentleman from us to be their next emperor!

My views have not changed since. These gentlemen have cost us many hundreds of thousands of dollars. I cannot see where we have derived any benefit at all commensurate with the expenditure. Rather it would appear to me that we should pay fifteen or twenty trade agents 310,000 a year each to promote trade between this country and Japan, China and the United States. speechtext: I am quite sure that what my right hon. friend has just said is wholly true. I hope he will not misunderstand the nature of my remark, or take it as an unwarranted criticism. The point I am particularly interested in making clear is this: there is a distinction between the diplomatic service and the service df the state in parliament and in administrations. I believe it would be unfortunate were it to be assumed, in the event of there being further legations established elsewhere, that just because someone was appointed a minister, he would necessarily be made a member of the privy council. I cannot think of any honour higher in the diplomatic world than that of being a minister plenipotentiary or an ambassador. It is an honour on a par with that of being a privy councillor in another field of public service. My point is that the two fields should be kept separate and distinct, and the fact that one is appointed to the diplomatic service should not necessarily mean his appointment as well to the privy council.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I have the consent of the house to revert to motions, I wish to introduce a motion with respect to the fourth report, which has been tabled, of the special committee appointed to investigate the Beau-hamois power project.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to dwell at length on the report of the special committee on the Beau-'harn'ois power project. The committee was set up by this house on the 10th of June last, and the reference contemplated that the
Beauharnois Power-Report

project known as the Beauharnois power project would be investigated from its inception by that committee, and that in addition to the investigation of the project the charges which were made by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) in May last should also be inquired into.
As hon. members know, the committee held its sessions from day to day, and invited and compelled the attendance of all witnesses who they thought might be able to contribute useful testimony in connection with the inquiry.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make this observation. Being chairman of this committee in the first regular session of the parliament of Canada in which I had the honour of being a member of this house, gave me no sense of gratification. The subject matters under review were very, very serious, so serious indeed that I accepted the duty of presiding over that committee only with a great deal of reluctance. Let me say at this juncture that I cannot do 'otherwise than commend the members of the committee for the attitude that they assumed throughout its deliberations. It was apparent that the investigation of necessity had to do with political matters, and it seems that when one's party is challenged or its actions are under fire it is difficult indeed to divorce oneself from the suggestion of partisanship, but the members of the committe, and particularly those belonging to the party opposite, adopted with a degree of resignation an attitude throughout which was commendable. I am beginning to find out that it is difficult when one is interested in politics to accept a position of this kind with any degree of resignation. However, the members of the committee did so conduct their duties that they made the work a great deal lighter than it might otherwise have been.
At the conclusion of our efforts I undertook the drafting of the committee's report. It was of necessity long and to some extent involved. On the last day of the committee's sittings I presented the report to the members of the committee, paragraph by paragraph and page by page, and the members of the committee studied it paragraph by paragraph and page by page. The committee went into the various statements of facts and the various inferences that were drawn- and let me say that inferences were not drawn from the facts unless those inferences were irresistible. I think the committee was careful to see that no one was involved unjustly or unfairly, and I experienced a degree of satisfaction when at the end of the review

of the draft report the members of the committee, representing all political parties in this house, were able to subscribe to its terms.
By reason of the unanimity which ultimately prevailed with respect to the report, and by reason of the length and the exhaustive nature of the inquiry as disclosed in the report, I do not feel that in introducing the motion that the house concur in the report I should dwell at any great length on the matters disclosed therein. The report speaks for iteslf. We had to deal with the disposition of probably the greatest single natural, national resource that Canada has. When I say that I do not mean that the Soulanges section of the St. Lawrence river is iteslf the greatest, but it may be, and probably is the pivotal part of the St. Lawrence river which ultimately we hope will become a great deep sea waterway from the head of the lakes to the Atlantic ocean. That being so, I think all the members of the committee felt that we should detach ourselves from petty party consideration in the hope that our deliberations might contribute something to the nation in whatever steps the house might see fit to take with respect to this matter. I do not think I need dwell upon its importance. We hear from time to time of the great natural resources of Canada. Sometimes people speak of our great hinterland and our great resources, and they use those euphonious terms which probably do not mean anything so far as the knowledge of the person speaking is concerned. Our resources, in large measure, can be identified by those who have taken the time to inquire into them, and to try to limit or delimit them, as the case may be. I think we may all agree that the St. Lawrence river and its development is a question bigger than party; it is probably bigger than any contest which may arise between the Dominion and the provinces; it is something that is inseparably connected with the future of this great Dominion. Let me say then, at the outset-and I think I am speaking the mind and reflecting the views of the committee-that there will be no conflict between the Dominion of Canada, the federal government, and the province of Quebec. The rights of that province will be religiously preserved. Undoubtedly they have rights- some of them may not be clearly defined- but I think I am reflecting the mind of the government and of the committee when I say that whatever steps may be taken in the future-and I trust and hope that by agreement, if possible steps may be taken-will be

Beauharnois Power-Report
with a view to conserving this national 'resource for the best interests of the people of Canada.
The Soulanges section of the St. Lawrence river, and the particular part of it with which your committee dealt-that portion lying between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis, a distance of fourteen or fifteen miles -constitutes probably, if engineers are to be relied upon-and I have no reason to suggest that they are not to be relied upon- the one portion of the St. Lawrence river most easily capable of being converted to the use of mankind, with respect both to power and to navigation. The total area of the river at this point lies within the limits of the province of Quebec. It is adjacent to the city and port of Montreal, and will undoubtedly constitute part of a deep sea waterway. The development of this project, I believe, can be carried on, having regard both to the navigability of the river and to the utilization of the power incidental thereto. I have no reason to suggest that the plan at present under way is not the soundest method of developing that section of the river, although engineers differ on that point. I am not sufficiently well acquainted with engineering problems, however, to take a stand on one side or the other. Having had with the other members of the committee an opportunity to visit the scene of the works and to visualize what is being done and what will be accomplished when the project is completed, I could not help but be impressed by the magnitude of the work and of its ultimate benefit, not only to the part of the country in and around that portion of the province of Quebec, but to the whole of the Dominion of Canada.
In dealing with this matter your committee felt they should direct their attention to various phases. With that in mind they went into the history of this power development as well as into questions affecting title. Probably the historical facts are important only from a historical point of view; at any rate there came a time about twenty years ago when those who had acquired what rights were originally in the former owners who held possession over one hundred years ago, found that the rights they held were manifestly important, although in themselves, at the inception, they were insignificant. In 1902 the Robert family caused to be incorporated, under the provisions of the Quebec Companies Act, a company known as the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company. They had utilized some power through a feeder that ran from lake St. Francis in a southeasterly
direction to the St. Louis river for the purpose of adding some volume to that stream, and providing power for the water wheels they had established upon it.
As we all know, about this time the development of -hydro-electric power became interesting from many angles. The whole of this continent was interested in hydro developments, and it must have been obvious- as it was to those who knew of this situation- -that nature had thrown in the lap of Canada one of the greatest resources that this or any other country ever possessed. The time had come when industry advanced to the stage that absorption of the powers to be developed from the Soulanges section could reasonably be anticipated. The time was then, and then only, ripe for the development of this enterprise.
Certain advances were made by the Robert people through the government of the province of Quebec with respect to the identification of their rights. After some litigation in the Exchequer Court of Canada about the year 1909 their rights were in a measure determined. Nothing further of consequence was done, although from -time to time in other reaches 'of the river adjacent thereto rights were acquired by certain companies to carry on comparatively insignificant industrial operations. It was not until the year 1923 that any pointed interest-and I use that word advisedly-was taken in connection with this development. True, back in 1912 Mr. Sweezey, at the suggestion of Sir Max Aitken, now Lord Beaveibrook, made some investigations with respect to this power project which, however, seemed to come -to nothing, and the project apparently was not seriously taken in hand until about 1923.
At that time a rather important event took place which I shall not dwell upon. I shall give merely a narrative history of the facts, because bon. members of the house are as capable as I am-probably more so-of drawing conclusions from the facts. Mr. Henry, who was in 1923 an employee of the Canadian National Railways, a man of quite superior engineering ability and, I think, equipped with a profound knowledge of the Sit. Lawrence river and all its possibilities, enlisted with him Mr. W. L. McDougald, the idea being to have Mr. Henry make an investigation into the possibilities of developing power by a canal extending from lake St. Francis to lake St. Louis. Mr. Henry ait that time was busy with his work in connection with the Canadian National Railways and is said to have employed another engineer for the purpose of making a survey between the two

lakes. There followed as a result the incorporation in Ottawa by the firm of Mc-Giverin, Haydon & Ebbs of a company known as the Sterling Industrial Corporation. That was accomplished on the fifth day of July, 1924.
Concurrently with its incorporation in fact on the same day, application was miade to the Department of Public Works, and two days later, on the 7th of July, a similar application was made to the Department of Railways and Canals, asking on behalf of this company that approval be granted under the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act to the plans then submitted, which Contemplated the diversion of 30,000 cubic feet per second from lake St. Francis down through a proposed canal to reenter the St. Lawrence river at lake St. Louis. Very shortly after the filing of this application advice was given to the promoters, or to their solicitors, that the application could not be entertained; and in that advice certain things were suggested that they might or might not do, whichever course they chose to adopt. At any rate, nothing was done. That application was allowed to lie there and was not renewed until some years later.
In 1927 Mr. Sweezey became interested in this project. Mr. Sweezey is unquestionably an engineer of repute. He, in my view, and I think it is the view of the other members of the committee, is a very capable engineer. But I must confess that he adopted a rather strange attitude on his first move towards acquiring the rights that he hoped to acquire on the St. Lawrence river. I have reference to the letter-with which hon. members are well acquainted, I think-to Alderic Raymond, in which he set out his conception of the method and the manner and the means that should be adopted and employed in order to accomplish the acquisition of the rights in this part of the river. No one could read that communication without at once being struck by Mr. Sweezey's conception of what might or might not be done if "political influence," as he calls it, could be assembled to his assistance. Now, right from the beginning-and in making this statement I am sure that the members of the committee will not quarrel with it

Mr. Sweezey and those who were associated with him seemed not only to be inspired, but to feel that they could make no headway unless they had political influence, and they proceeded upon that assumption, so that even those who had no political influence at all, even those who were not in t'he counsels of any party, probably participated in the disbursement of moneys at the hands of the promoters. It 
is 'not a pleasant thing to contemplate, but that seems to have been the case. From 1927 onwards we find $437,000 paid in legal fees. Of course, they were noit legal fees in the sense of payments for professional services rendered, and that became manifest as the investigation proceeded.
Application was made to the federal government at Ottawa for the approval of certain plans on behalf of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company after the option to acquire the stock of that company had been secured by Mr. Sweezey. That application met with considerable opposition. Other power interests on the river, jealous, I presume, of the rights sought to be acquired by the Sweezey organization, set up an opposition that at one time, according to the evidence, almost spelled disaster for his application. But there came a time when this opposition seemed to lose their interest in opposing, and almost overnight they reappeared in another form, namely, in support of the application which they had theretofore so vigorously opposed.
Out of it all came the passing of the order in council we have heard so much about,
P.C. 422. The order in council, shortly stated, gave the right, or assumed to give the right, to divert 40,000 cubic feet per second from lake St. Francis into a canal down to lake St. Louis. Prior to this Mr. Henry had taken on a new duty; he still remained associated with the Canadian National Railways, but he was appointed deputy Minister of the Department of Railways and Canals, and during the time he occupied that office three orders in council were passed whereby the water in the river which the Montreal Cotton Company had the right to use was acquired by the Sweezey interests. There may be a difference of opinion as to the efficacy of the order in council, whether it in fact gives the right that those who were sponsoring the application hoped it did give. Your committee felt that it was not within the purview of the task assigned to it and that it would serve no useful purpose for it to try to define the law with respect to that order in council.
But it is plain that the order in council, by its terms, contemplated that nothing should be done in this stretch of the river until the final detailed plans had been approved by the minister. Those final detailed plans were not approved, and I believe I am stating it fairly when I say they have not been approved to this day. But the work went on. It is only fair at this juncture to point out that evidence was given, and with a good deal of force, that detailed plans, that

Beauharnois Power-Report
is, working plans, could not very well be prepared and approved that would not have to be changed as the work progressed. I say that in fairness to those who were sponsoring the application. But the fact remains that the plans contemplated by the order in council were not approved and have not been approved up to the present time.
Another point I might touch on in passing is this: that the land through which this canal will run from lake St. Francis to lake St. Louis is all owned by the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company Limited. As the case stands at present there will be no fight as between provinces or as between the Dominion and any province or anyone else with respect to the bed or banks of the new canal because they are owned in fee simple by the company.
That raises another point, if one cares to pursue it further, with respect to the three bridges crossing the channel. The Navigable Waters Protection Act itself does not in any of its sections, so far as I am able to read and interpret them, give to the governor in council power to authorize the diversion of water from a navigable stream. It is quite true that the evidence disclosed that, in the past, rightly or wrongly, approval has been given to such diversions, but that raises just the point whether or not, under that act, the governor in council had the right to do what they did. At any rate, granted they had the right and that ultimately the waters are turned into the canal and the total useful flow of the St. Lawrence river is made use of- and that is what was in contemplation by the promoters, and what is still in contemplation according to the evidence-then we will have the rather curious situation of a new river built from lake St. Francis to lake St. Louis, the bed and banks of which are owned by a private corporation and across which are three bridges. The Navigable Waters Protection Act, if I remember section 11, distinctly states that no approval shall be given under the act to the construction of a bridge across the St. Lawrence river.
The authority of parliament comes from the British North America Act; section 91, with which I am sure hon. members of the house are well acquainted, deals with navigation and shipping. The power there given for the control of navigation and shipping is given to the parliament of Canada, and the words are just as I have used them. Of course, the widest interpretation can be given those two words. The Navigable Waters Protection Act was passed by this house under the authority conferred upon this parliament by the British
North America Act with respect to navigation and shipping, and under the terms of the Navigable Waters Protection Act certain authority is delegated to the governor in council. In my view at least that does not include the power to authorize the diversion of water from a navigable stream. However, I may be wrong in that; others may take a different view, but that was one of the matters your committee had under review and upon which they felt they could not make any useful pronouncement.
The next step in connection with the matter with which your committee had to deal was the structure of the various syndicates and companies. I am not going to labour that phase of the question, because the history is set out in the report which was read in the house a day or two ago. I think it is only necessary to say that one syndicate was formed with 5.000 authorized part interests or units; that a little later another syndicate was formed with 30,000 part interests or units; that the second syndicate took over the first, giving two shares for one, and that the assets Which were originally those of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, namely, the shares of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, which were acquired by the first syindicate and subsequently by the second syndicate, were in turn transferred to a new corporation known as the Beauhamois Power Company, Limited, a company incorporated under the Dominion Companies Act.
Following out what appeared to be the course Mr. Sweezey set himself, in order to procure the rights that he wanted he got the financial support, and I think I am not unfair in saying the political support, of different gentlemen. He obtained the financial support of Frank P. Jones and the political and financial support of Senator Raymond and Hon. Walter Mitchell. Later on those gentleman were joined by Senator McDougald, whose advent into this project appeared to come about in this way: If hon. members will remember, a moment or two ago I said that he and Mr. Henry incorporated the Sterling Industrial Corporation and filed plans on July 5, 1904. Those plans remained in the department. When Mr. Sweezey started in to * acquire these rights to develop the power on the St. Lawrence, Mr. Henry-and I think I am not unfair in stating it in this way-apparently was watching the developments and he, acting on behalf of himself and Senator McDougald, interviewed Mr. Sweezey, or Mr. Sweezey interviewed Mr. Henry. The evidence is not clear as to which one was

Beauhamois Power-Report
interviewing the other, but it was a sparring match, as it were, to get information one from the other. The ultimate result was that Mr. Sweezey became convinced that in order to have his efforts crowned with success he would have to get rid of the application of the Sterling Industrial Corporation, which was owned by Senator McDougald and by Mr. Henry, who at that time or shortly afterwards was the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals. A good deal of evidence was taken with respect to those interviews, and with regard to what was done before an agreement was reached. Some of the evidence was vague, but during the taking of that evidence there came a time-and the evidence can be referred to by any hon. member-^ when a question was put to Mr. Henry substantially to this effect: "Is it correct that you filed that application for the rights which are now under discussion for the purpose of compelling anyone who might thereafter undertake the development of that section of the St. Lawrence river to take care of McDougald and Henry?" His answer was, "I guess you can put it that way."
Those interests became very valuable, the upshot being that 2,000 part interests in the new syndicate were given in exchange for them. Evidence was taken with respect to what consideration was given for the issue of those 2,000 part interests, and that evidence was not contradicted. On both sides it was reluctantly admitted that there was no consideration; and in fact it got down to being described as a nuisance value and similar units in that same syndicate were sold for $550 each.
Those matters of necessity had to be inquired into by your committee, and again I wish to commend members of the committee for the ability they displayed and for the self-abnegation, if I may put it that way, as far as party politics were concerned, which they showed in their desire to search out and attempt to determine what was the truth in connection with this promotion. It is, I believe, the opinion of the committee, and it is reflected in the report, that this project or a similar project is one that will be of great advantage to this country and, if properly built, will become part of the deep sea waterway. Whether or not there was too much hurry in the building, your committee does not see fit to report upon except indirectly. At any rate, it was the view of the committee that the work was a very important one and that we could not report otherwise than to say that every safeguard should be taken so that the work might not be im-

perilled, and at the same time that the rights of the province of Quebec and of the people of Canada should be protected.
I will not go further in discussing the financial structure or set-up of the laslt company. There were five management shares that contemplated continuity of management for a period of ten years. Probably it is a wise precaution to take if the management is in sound hands during the initial stage. There were common class A and class B nonvoting shares. These, in the main, were given those who were raising money, and they in turn subscribed for some of the shares with the profits they made out of various syndicates. The final result was that the promoters of the company, who now own and control the company, have no money in it and have made a great profit out of it. I am not complaining of that if the rights of the people of this country are adequately protected. It is for the members of the house, after a review of the report, for concurrence in which I shall presently move, to say whether or not that protection has been given.
There is one oTher phase of the matter which I wish to discuss, probably the one phase that is most difficult of all. I refer to the employment of moneys out of this project for the purpose of contributing to campaign funds of political parties. I know from my reading-not from my association with politics, because that has been but a recent matter with me1-'that contributions to campaign funds to all parties have been made for many, many years, and I do not think the leaders of any party would care to suggest that funds, large or small as they may be, are not made to organize the voters of the country in order that the views of the party particularly concerned might prevail. That has been the custom. Whether or not it is a proper one, I do not think I am called upon to pass judgment. At any rate it has been done, and I assume that it will be done in the future. It costs something to organize the vote of the voters of the country. Whether it is done properly or improperly is probably the important question. Those who contribute to the campaign funds of the parties, and do so prompted by their belief in the soundness of the policy of the particular party, can be, I think, probably excused and, maybe, commended. But those who contribute to a party's coffers, inspired only by the hope- and in time something more than hope-that they will, by reason thereof, be able through the influence of that party to alienate from the people of the country the resources that belong to them-those contributions, I say,

Beauhamois Power-Report
and those who make them cannot be too strongly condemned.
In connection with this project I must confess that I am unable to divorce myself from the view that the contributions to campaign funds that were made from t'he company's funds, which came from the sale of bonds to the people, were made for the purpose of influencing those who might be returned to power; and those who took them, those who collected them, receive in the committee's report the condemnation they deserve.
This is the first unit in the course of the development of this great natural national resource. Obstacles were thrown in the way here and thrown in the way there, purely and simply because those who were doing it felt that they would be paid to step aside. Now, this is only t'he first step, and every time a dollar is added to the capital cost of any business the ultimate result is that those who have to transact business with that company or with that industry must, all down through the future, just pay that much more for the product of that industry. Therefore it is very essential, particularly in the development of a resource such as this, that its initial capital cost be kept down to the lowest possible limit, in order that the benefits that will flow from its development will be reaped by the people of the country. This is only the first unit, and if, on examination of the report, you can visualize what might have happened if, as each recurring application came along for the diversion of more waters of the river, the same course was taken, then I ask you to realize for yourselves the load that this resource would carry before it was finally developed. We should have on our hands a burden which probably would in large measure discount the benefit and advantage that nature has given us by placing that water available to the people of the country.
I have spoken longer than I intended and I trust that in the remarks I have made I have not departed from the evidence that was disclosed before the committee. Our report in certain respects may be blunt, but it is supported by the cold, unvarnished, sworn testimony, and your committee a sics this house to concur in that report. I now move, seconded by Mr. Dupre, that the report be concurred in.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Gordon), who has just moved for concurrence in the report which has been presented to the house, has outlined its main
features. In doing so he indicated that the report has several important divisions. The first is historical in character, reviewing the inception and development of the Beauhamois canal project. The next division has to do with the organization of syndicates in connection with the promotion of the company, while another portion of the report has to do With individuals who were concerned in its promotion, and particularly with the fees which were paid to many lawyers whom the promoters seemed to believe had a certain political influence which they should seek in this manner to gain. The minister has indicated that the report further deals with the question of contributions to party funds, and while he did not mention it, I think I am right in stating that the report concludes with certain important recommendations which this house is asked to accept.
Perhaps I could not do better than to follow the minister in his order of presentation and to deal with the matter not only in the sequence he has pursued but more particularly with respect to the particular topics which he has touched upon, leaving other matters aside for the present, unless perchance some seem to me to be deserving of special mention.
I would like to do as the committee has done, present to the house a statement as to the position of the late government in granting approval of the plans of the Beauhamois company in the light of the perspective which governed in the matter. In so doing I hope the house will not feel that I am trespassing unduly upon its time if I outline the background, so to speak, of the- developments in which the approval of the plans of the Beauhamois canal had its particular setting. After all, I assume that what the house and the country is most interested in is whether the late administration, of which I had the honour to be the head, granted approval of the plans from any motive other than that of the public interest, whether the decision was a wise one, whether all that could be expected of the ministry in the way of safeguarding its action was or was not performed. It is from that point of view that I wish to develop what I have to say.
When the late Liberal administration assumed office there were many pressing problems facing this country. Not the least important of these were the differences which had sprung up in the course of years between some of the provinces and the Dominion government itself. These were not differences of a character to involve conflict between governments, but there was a feeling on the part

Beauhamois Power-Report
of some of the provinces that they had not received full justice in matters with respect to which the Dominion had more or less the determining voice. As an administration we set ourselves the task of endeavouring to remove these differences as largely and as completely as possible, believing that upon Canadian unity more than upon anything else depended the progress and development of our country.
Among the questions which were to the fore and which occupied the time and thought of the ministry perhaps more than any other during the first few years after it assumed office was the question of the return to the western provinces of their natural resources. This question had been facing the governments for many years, and it was one with which we wrestled and of which we finally successfully disposed. Allied in a way to that question was a grievance on the part of the province of British Columbia. That province felt that it had been deprived of certain lands along the Canadian Pacific railway and in the Peace River belt, and that those lands should be restored to it. That question also was dealt with, and may I say, dealt with successfully. We had not been in office very long before difficulties which were latent asserted themselves in the maritime provinces, and we were confronted with a great deal in the way of social unrest, and a feeling on the part of those provinces that they had not been properly treated from the time they had come into the federation. As hon. members know, we appointed the Duncan commission to investigate the grievances of the maritime provinces. When that commission made its report we acted upon it, if not in its entirety, at least with respect to all its major features. So far as the other provinces were concerned, Ontario and Quebec, there remained very few differences or difficulties of any kind with which to deal, with the exception of the question of the navigation of the St. Lawrence river and the development of power on that river. In the case of Ontario that question was particularly involved because it had to do with international ns well as national considerations; it had as I have indicated also to do with power as well as navigation. A vexed question was the degree to which the Dominion itself might have ownership of the power which would result from any improvements which it might make with respect to navigation. These were the problems with which we were occupied at the time the Beauharnois application came before the administration.

I think I need scarcely say to any body of hon. members of this house that a government comes to know of questions only as they are presented to the ministry for consideration. There are at the present moment innumerable matters awaiting consideration in the different departments of government but they will not assume importance, so far as the government of the day is concerned, until they reach the cabinet through the minister of the department in which they happen to arise. The first real concern which the administration had with the Beauharnois canal was when the formal application which had been made to the Department of Public Works for the approval of the plans came from that department before the cabinet for consideration. That however was not the first intimation which individual members of the government had had of an application being made for the approval of plans for the Beauharnois canal project.
Perhaps the house will permit me to speak more particularly of my own knowledge of the matter, giving, as I speak, my version as one who at the time was holding the office of Prime Minister. I have a very slight recollection of having heard anything about the Beauharnois canal project, so called, before I was asked by Mr. Frank P. Jones if 1 would grant him an interview to discuss a matter of considerable importance. I did not know at the time very much about the matter that Mr. Jones wished to discuss, but he wrote me upon it and I arranged to accord him an interveiw. That was in June, if I remember rightly, or July, 1&28. Mr. Jones called on me at my office and we had a Short conversation. My mind was full at the time of the question of the St. Lawrence development, the deep seaway. It was a matter to which the administration had been giving a good deal of attention. We were in communication with the government of the United States with respect to it. As hon. members know, the exchange of correspondence between the two governments had been tabled in the house. My first reaction to the interview I 'had with Mr. Jones was as to just how this particular project might affect the St. Lawrence waterway. In that connection I put to him the very direct question: How would the province of Ontario view a matter of this kind? Because I knew that the province of Ontario had been interested in seeking to get approval of certain plans of power development on the international section of the St. Lawrence, and that we had not been able, as a government, to see our way to grant that approval until our exchange of

Beauhamois Power-Report
views with the government of the United States had progressed a greater length than they had. Being international waters the consent of both countries was needed. I felt that if the government was even to consider the project at all, we would have to feel perfectly sure that out of our consideration there was not going to arise any difference or possibility of estrangement between two of the provinces, but rather that whatever would be done would accord with our policy of seeking to remove altogether whatever in the way of differences might exist between the provinces and the Dominion.
In 1928, as members will recall, the Briand-Kellogg peace pact was signed in Paris. I had the honour of representing this country at its signature, and subsequently of representing Canada at the assembly and on the council of the League of Nations. Those particular missions occupied a considerable portion of my time abroad that year. Being absent, I had no further thought of the Beauhamois matter until after my return to Canada, when the matter again came up for consideration. Shortly after my return to Canada I received another letter from Mr. Jones, in which he recalled the previous interview and the question that I had put to him at the time. He said that he was in a position to answer the question, and he enclosed certain correspondence in his letter, which correspondence was tabled in this house, I think, two years ago, which answered the question which I had put to him. It was shortly after that, that the application came before the government for consideration.
May I pause here to say a word-I shall enlarge upon it a little later-as to the attitude which I have taken with regard not only to the Beauharnois project but to every question that came before the cabinet during the time that I was Prime Minister; for this has a very important bearing on all that pertains to the consideration of this application. Once a matter came before the government for consideration, I made it religiously a rule not to discuss it with anyone-whether members of the House of Commons on my own side, friends of the party from outside, or anyone else-other than my colleagues. I received respectfully such representations as were made to me, but I invariably made the reply: this is a question under consideration in the cabinet; it will be dealt with on its merits;
I cannot discuss this question with you. I am afraid that many of my own followers were most impatient at times, or perhaps I should say more than patient with me in
this attitude, I know that they have felt, and it has reached my ears very often, that I was inaccessible, that it was difficult for members of the party even to have a chance to discuss with me many of the questions which they were concerned in. Part of that has been due to the fact, which I am sure my right hon. friend will be able to bear out as true, that the task of a Prime Minister is a very considerable one, and that any man who wishes to master the questions that have to be discussed in this House of Commons, unless he has had extensive preparation and unless he has a powerful mind, will require pretty much all the time he can get to himself to study intimately and thoroughly the essentials of the problems that come before his government and before parliament for consideration. I have all along been conscious of my own limitations in dealing with many of the great questions which involved complicated legal as well as technical considerations, and it has probably taken me much longer than it might have taken other men to become thoroughly familiar with the different questions that have been discussed in the cabinet and on the floor of this house; but I found that the only way in which it could be done was in just the manner I have indicated. I have been prepared to be misunderstood on the part of my own following, and even to incur the reproaches of many of the best supporters of the party, because I have been unwilling to discuss with them matters which were before the cabinet council for its consideration. I have told them I would not very frankly and emphatically. Indeed, I think every secretary who I have had will bear me out when I say that the instruction that I have oftenest given is not to let anyone into my office until he knew what he wanted to see me about, and unless it was something that could be told to my secretary then I preferred to have my office to myself. That has been pretty much the rule I followed during the time I was Prime Minister. It may serve to account for an attitude, which some of my own followers have not always appreciated. I mention that now because when this application came before the cabinet there were many persons who did try to see me and did want to discuss with me the question of the Beauhamois canal project. They were not only those who wanted to see the project plans approved; they were very powerful interests that were concerned about this power not going to the Beauharnois people. Certain of these claimed they were friends of the party-if it may be
435S

Beauharnois Power-Report
expressed in those terms-or professed to be, and thought for that reason they should be entitled to present their views. I dealt with all in exactly the same way. On this question, as on all others-I am not singling out this one, because my attitude as Prime Minister in this instance was exactly the same as it has been with regard to every other question -I refused to discuss the subject then before the cabinet with other than my colleagues, preferring to get my knowledge of the situation from what might be said at the council table.
For that reason the decision which was reached in cabinet council, so far as I personally was concerned-and I think I can say the same with respect to my colleagues of the day-was a decision reached as the result of open discussion across the council table in which every conceivable aspect and consideration was thoroughly discussed, and the merits thereof very carefully weighed. In a few minutes I shall go into the considerations of which we had to take aocount. Before doing that however may I give to the house by way of confirmation of what I have said, and to throw a little more light on the subject, one or two communications to which I have referred.
These communications were tabled as the result of a return for all correspondence between the government of Canada and other parties under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, in relation to the question commonly known as the Beauharnois power and canal project. An order was granted by the house on February 13 or 14, 1929, for these papers. It includes all the correspondence that was in my office at the time. The letter from Mr. Jones to which I have referred is dated at Montreal, June 22, 1928, and is as follows:
Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa. Ont.
Dear Sir:
For the past month I have been desirous of seeing you regarding the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, but have refrained from asking for an interview, knowing how frightfully busy you must have been while the house was sitting, and although I know your time is really more than fully taken up now, necessity compels me to ask if you would, if possible, be kind enough to grant me a halfhour's interview as early next week as you can.
You will remember I told you before I sailed for Europe I expected to take an active interest in the Beauharnois proposition, this X am doing, but naturally do not want it to drag, and I would like if you would make it possible to have actual construction work started this fall. I am anxious to see this water go through
[Mr. Mackenzie King.l
the turbines and industries using the power generated. I may be impetuous, but I have always found that while impetuosity may be a drawback to an individual, it is very often good for the community.
I have the honour to be,
Your obedient servant,
F. P. Jones.
I arranged for the interview with Mr. Jones and at the interview made to him the representations to which I have already referred. The next communication I received from him was dated at Ottawa, November 28, 1928, from the Chateau Laurier, and is as follows:
Right Hon. W. L. M. King, P.C.,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir:
At the last interview you were kind enough to give me, re Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, it was suggested that I might procure some evidence as to the attitude of the government of Ontario towards the proposed power development. This I have done and therefore would like, if it is possible, to have you grant me a short interview in which 1 could submit the evidence to you.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
F. P. Jones.
Unfortunately Mr. Jones did not receive an interview. He, however, sent me another communication. This one was dated from the Chateau Laurier, Ottawa, November 30, 1928, and is as follows:
Rt. Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, P.C., M.P., Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
Sir:
You will recall that when I saw you a few months ago regarding the application of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company for the approval of its plans under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, you asked me regarding the attitude of the premiers of Quebec and Ontario regarding this project.
I was in a position to assure you that not only the premier but the entire government of Quebec was practically unanimously in favour of it and anxious to see the development go ahead. I could not, however, state definitely the precise attitude of the premier of Ontario.
1 now take the liberty of enclosing a copy of a letter from the Hon. Mr. Ferguson, dated November 19, to the Hon. Mr. Taschereau, by which you will see that Hon. Mr. Ferguson considers that the matter is one which should be dealt with according to the wishes of the province of Quebec. Mr. Ferguson appreciates the spirit of cooperation shown by the province of Quebec, and evidently feels that this development will be beneficial to Ontario, inasmuch as it will be an additional source of supply of power to help satisfy Ontario's rapidly increasing demand.
I think the letter of the Hon. Mr. Ferguson justifies my stating to you that Ontario, as well as Quebec, is in favour of the project.

Beauharnois Power-Report
I -svish to state that the copy of this letter which I enclose was sent to me by Mr. Tasche-reau, and I have his permission to give it to you.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
S'. P. Jones.
The letter which was enclosed is before me. I shall not read the whole of it, because it deals with two subjects but shall read that part dealing with the Beauharnois canal project. It is from the Hon. Howard Ferguson, at the time Prime Minister of Ontario, and is addressed to Mr. Taschereau the Prime Minister of Quebec. It is as follows:
I note you say that the Beauharnois people are about to press the Dominion authorities to give effect to the legislation passed by your legislature at the last session. I fully realize that this development is entirely within the boundaries of the province of Quebec and this province has no voice in the matter. We do, however, greatly appreciate the spirit of cooperation in the development of these two great old provinces which you have so frequently shown, and which is again evidenced by the provision you have made that a portion ol this power may be made available to this province should we need it and are able to negotiate a favourable contract, so long as it is not directly or indirectly exported to the United States.
Owing to the undoubted delay there will be in regard to the settlement of the development of the St. Lawrence and Ottawa river powers, and the rapidly increasing demand for power in Ontario, I feel that we will probably again in the near future have to take advantage of your good-will and secure a further supply from some point in your province.
I am sure I need not assure you again, as I have done in the past, of our appreciation of your attitude towards Ontario and her power problems by voluntarily making such generous provision a condition of your approval of the IJeauharnois undertaking. If I am right in my view as to our early requirements of power, Beauharnois would seem to me to be a very convenient and favourable point from which to procure our requirements.
Yours faithfully,
G. H. Ferguson.
I believe the correspondence I have read is sufficient to make clear the fact that in November, or the beginning of December 1928, the administration of the day was in this position: They had before them an application from a company which had been organized in the province of Quebec, had received its charter from the province of Quebec, had been given a lease of power from the province of Quebec, had been given the right to divert certain waters from the province of Quebec, that the Premier of Ontario knew of the particulars of the lease granted and the conditions attached to it, and had
stated in a written communication which I assume was intended to be brought to the attention of the federal government, that he approved of the project, that he would be in need of additional power for his own province and that he would probably have to make a contract at an early date with the government of Quebec in order to get the power he needed for the province of Ontario. That was the position as it presented itself to the cabinet. Our first consideration was whether we could afford to ignore the wishes of the two provinces most vitally affected in this power development, provided that ail requirements with respect to the federal obligation of approving the -plans were fully met.
Now, may I pause at 'this point to remind hon. -members what was the obligation, the duty and the power of the federal government in this particular. We were not required to pass upon the organization of a company, in the application before us we had nothing to do with leasing the power, we had nothing to do with the diversion of water; all this belonged to the government of the province of Quebec-a government just as sovereign within its jurisdiction as the Dominion government within its jurisdiction. We had to consider whether, when the government of Quebec, and I might add the government of Ontario, were urging that these plans should be approved, we were justified in refusing approval. We had to consider, -when the government of the province of Ontario was asserting its needs for more power, whether we were justified by refusing such approval, thereby to prevent the Ontario government from getting that extra power from the source with which it said it was going to make a contract. Our obligation was limited to the approval of the plans from the point of view of the protection of navigation. The protection of navigation comes within the jurisdiction of this federal parliament. Our obligation was in the nature of an administrative act certifying that the grant made by the province of Quebec with respect to water powers within its own jurisdiction would not in any way interfere with navigation on the St. Lawrence.
But we had a larger question to consider- and this, let me repeat, was the thought mostly in the minds of the administration, because it was a question that we had been dealing with for four or five years,-namely, the question of the ultimate development of the St. Lawrence deep seaway project. We had to make perfectly sure not only that any project we were going to approve would not interfere with navigation, but that it would
Beauharnois Power-Report

be so carried out that it would not interfere with but rather further the development of the St. Lawrence deep sea waterway. It was to that question that we had to direct our attention particularly.
In that connection we had to take into account all outstanding considerations of importance. First of all we had to consider whether, in constructing works for the protection of navigation, power developed from those particular works would belong to the Dominion or to the province. There never was any question about the power in the St. Lawrence river within the province of Quebec itself belonging to that province. The question for our consideration was whether once the works necessary for the protection of navigation, were constructed, and power developed therefrom, that power should belong to the province of Quebec or to the dominion. That was a legal question that we were not in a position to pronounce upon except through the advice of the law officers of the crown.
Here again may I revert to the original setting of this matter. As I have said, the question of the settlement of the differences with respect to the St. Lawrence development was the outstanding question with Ontario and Quebec. When the Dominion-provincial conference met in 1927, the year of the diamond jubilee of confederation, the premiers of Ontario and Quebec asked that this question of the relative jurisdiction and rights of the dominion and the provinces respectively with regard to power on the St. Lawrence should be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada. As a result of that request a series of questions was prepared and after amendment submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada. Those questions were before the court when the application of the Beauharnois Power Company came before our government, but no decision upon them was given until the eve of the meeting of parliament in February, 1929. I ask hon. members tO' keep that fact also in mind-that the question of the respective rights of the Dominion and the provinces with regard to power developments in all their phases was before the supreme court at that time.
When the opinion of the supreme court on the question submitted to it was delivered, I confess that not being a lawyer I could not make head or tail of it, and much to my relief I found that even members of the legal profession were in the same quandary that is in so far as the opinion being of a character which would settle the question of legal rights. In a word, as I recollect it, the supreme court said it could not decide a hypothetical case,

that the question of legal rights could only be finally determined when a concrete case was before the court. '
We had then to consider whether or not all this power development should be held up indefinitely simply because we had not a definite finding on the points submitted to the supreme court. However, the court laid down very definitely certain principles, and those principles were a guide of the administration. What we eventually decided to do was this. So far as the province of Quebec was concerned, there seemed to be no doubt whatever that the power developed within the provincial area belonged to that province. We undertook to say that any power resulting from the works that were constructed for the purpose of protecting navigation should be treated as though it belonged to the province of Quebec, even although the legal decision to that effect had not been given. But in order to be fair with all concerned, we took precisely the same position with regard to the province of Ontario. We said to Ontario: while we cannot give you a legal right in respect to these matters, we will treat you as though you had that legal right. In other words, in dealing with Ontario power rights we were prepared to treat the province of Ontario in precisely the same way as we were prepared to treat the province of Quebec.
At the time that we were awaiting the decision of the supreme court we were in conference with Premier Ferguson of Ontario and Premier Taschereau of Quebec, and members of the Dominion government, with a view to seeing if we could not mutually agree upon terms that would be acceptable to the provinces as well as to ourselves. We had two conferences. After the first conference we believed we had everything satisfactorily settled. Apparently the premiers of the two provinces went away feeling that we had said we would concede what they contended were their legal rights, whereas our contention was that we could not say what their legal rights were but we would treat them as though they had the legal rights they asserted though we were not in a position to give them legal rights. The whole purpose of the conference was to enable us to meet the situation by way of conference rather than as a matter of law.
We had a second conference which was held, if I recollect aright, on the day the decision of the supreme court was given out. At that conference I drew up and presented in the form of a definite memorandum the attitude the federal government was prepared to take in dealing with the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. By way of confirmation of what I

Beauhamois Power-Report
am now stating, may I refer to a file of correspondence which took place between Premier Ferguson of Ontario, Premier Taschereau of Quebec and myself in arranging for these conferences. Without going into the correspondence at any length may I quote the essential points from these communications. The first is under date of April 17, 1928, and is a communication relating to the St. Lawrence waterway development. I sent to Mr. Ferguson, Premier of Ontario, a letter having the following as its concluding paragraph:
In our view, as the correspondence indicates, the next step should be conferences with the governments of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. I hope that it will prove convenient for you to take part in such a discussion, as to which T shall write you more definitely at the close of the session.
I must correct one statement I have made. Aifter that communication which was dated April 17, 1928, Mr. Ferguson, owing to reasons which he outlined in subsequent corespond1-ence, indicated that he was not able to come down for a conference at the time, and the conferences which I said had taken place in 1929 I should have said took place in 1930. In the meantime however there was correspondence, which I have under my hand, showing the extent to which we were proceeding with both provinces in the same way. For example, on May 3,	1928, Premier
Ferguson wrote as follows:
Some four or five years ago this government, through its electrical agency, the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario, filed with the proper department at Ottawa plans for the development of power on the international section of the St. Lawrence river. We requested the approval of these plans and at intervals since that time have urged that early action be taken towards such approval. We still await a favourable reply. The government of Ontario feels that the power problem is the most pressing, and is quite separate and distinct from the question of international navigation project. No matter what may be the outcome of the negotiations for the canalization of the St. Lawrence, it would appear that many years must elapse before the project can be completed.
As I have explained, questions of power and of navigation were so inseparably intertwined with regard to the international section of the St. Lawrence that as a government we felt it impossible to conclude any negotiations relating to the international section of the St. Lawrence at the time Mr. Ferguson hoped they might be concluded. One of the causes of the delay was a certain difference of view between the engineers of the province of Ontario and those of the Dominion with respect to what would be the best route for a canal, and in that connection we asked that a conference should be held between the engineers, which conference was delayed for a
time but finally took place, moving the project along a step further with regard to the St. Lawrence.
In a communication dated August 14, 1928, to Mr. Ferguson, among other things I pointed out the following:
This objective which you emphasize so strongly can be attained only through an adequate solution of the problems of engineering and finance, of constitutional authority and of international adjustments which are involved.
Consideration of the development of power from the St. Lawrence cannot be separated, you will agree, from consideration of the conservation and development of this great national asset for the paramount purposes of navigation and commerce.
Then again:
Nor can we overlook the difficulties as to jurisdiction involved by the division of authority under our federal system.
And a little further:	[DOT]
So marked has been the divergence of view as to legislative control and proprietary interest in connection with many phases of water-power development that the representatives of the province of Ontario at the recent Dominion-provincial conference joined in a request to the Dominion to submit a ease to the Supreme Court of Canada. This has been done, after consultation with provincial representatives, and the case will be heard at an early date. While it is not necessary to postpone all further action until the respective rights of the Dominion and the provinces have been judicially determined, it is obvious that the results of this appeal to the courts, undertaken at the request of the provinces and the full cooperation of the federal government, may affect very materially the view of either authority as to the feasibility of the various methods of construction and finance.
That bears out what I said as to one of the causes of delay in not being able to meet the situation as far as Ontario was concerned. I concluded that communication by saying:
I trust that in the way indicated we may find it possible to cooperate effectively for the advancement of the interests of the province of Ontario and of the Dominion as a whole.
I shall not go further into this correspondence, because it deals more particularly with the St. Lawrence development, but at the conference which was held in Ottawa with Premier Taschereau and Premier Ferguson, in the early part of last year, after we had approved the Beauhamois plans, we made a statement of our policy with respect to approval of plans generally and with respect to powers on the St. Lawrence. That memorandum was as follows:

Yes; but what I am trying to point out at the moment is that when we dealt with the Beauharnois matter we were trying to settle it in the light of what would apply to the whole of the St. Lawrence development. We were endeavouring to lay down principles which would govern with respect to any similar situation that might arise at any time. And I think I made that quite clear in this House of Commons when parliament met in February 1929.
I wish to touch briefly upon other important features which have a bearing on the matter. I need not say anything with respect to the different meetings of the cabinet beyond the fact that the application came before us first of all in the month of November. To safeguard our action, particularly with respect to the question of the diversion of water and our rights in that particular, we obtained from the law officers of the crown a written opinion on the subject. That written opinion appears in the records of the proceedings before the committee and I need not quote it at the moment. But I mention it to indicate that we were seeking the best legal opinion that we could obtain to guide us in our decision. After the Department of Justice had given its opinion the whole Beauharnois situation was considered in the light of that opinion. Later, when the supreme court gave its decision, the matter had again to be reviewed in the light of the opinion of that body, and it was not until after the supreme court had given its decision that it was possible to begin work on the final drafting of the order in council which contained the conditions that were imposed upon the canal people.
Now, parliament opened in 1929 on the 7th of February. And here I wish to speak particularly of what I regard as all important. In the course of the inquiry before the committee an effort was made, it seemed to me, to have it appear that there had been great delays in the granting of approval of this application-. As far as I can gather from a reading of the evidence, questions were asked in a way which sought to have it appear that this matter was being dragged on over a considerable period of time.

It never came before council for consideration until the month of November. Up to that time it had been a departmental matter, and Mr. Jones's letter makes it pretty plain that until he

spoke to me I had no knowledge that any application was in .the department. However, the point I am making now is that an effort has been made to have it appear that action was being delayed. The fact of the matter is that at the time the press of the country was asking-Why this haste? Why this hurry? All the while the course the cabinet was taking was one which would insure every possible safeguard. The promoters saw no reason why they should not get their approval before the supreme court gave its decision; and while waiting for that, they saw no reason why approval should not be given before parliament met. There were two very important considerations which the cabinet had to take into account. The position we took in council was that we would not grant approval of the application until we had before us the opinion of the supreme court. If the opinion of the supreme court had been adverse to what was being contemplated, that would have settled the matter; we should then have known definitely that our powers were restricted in the way indicated by the court. But when the opinion of the court came, it did not afford us very much light or guidance. The other consideration was the meeting of parliament. If we had approved the plans before parliament met, there is not a member on either side of the house who would not have said, ''Why all this hurry? Why did the government approve the plans before parliament met? Why could they not have waited? They knew we were meeting in February and they could have put it off until parliament met." Well, we did put it off, and I took care to let parliament know as soon as it assembled that we had this very matter under consideration.
I did so deliberately in order that every hon. member of the house might be. on his guard with respect to what was being done in the consideration of this particular project. I sought to indicate to parliament at that time what the considerations were of which we had to take account.
May I add this further point. There has been a good deal of talk about political considerations and influence in this matter. So far as I knew-and I think I am right-Mr. Jones, who was the prime mover in seeking to get the plans approved, was a strong Conservative, having been one all his life. I believed, in dealing with this matter, that the government was dealing with a Conservative corporation. That did not make any difference in our obligation; we had to view the question on its merits. But far from considering that we were approving any plans with which any political friends of the administration
were concerned, our conception, certainly mine, was that the main factors in the company were Mr. Jones and those who were associated with him. As regards Mr. Sweezey, I did not know what his politics were. I have never met him; I should not know him if he were to come into this room at this moment. That may be an unfortunate circumstance, but nevertheless it is true. I know nothing about his politics. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister told me last night the he understood Air. Sweezey was thought of as a Liberal candidate in the last election.
