Mr. Jones was the only man with whom I had discussed this matter. He surely had not the authority to negotiate in the way he did unless he was the prime mover in the matter. I knew Mr. Jones as a very able business man, one who was generally successful in what he was undertaking in the way of business and industrial

the government at the time had been moved by political influences or by any consideration of the kind with respect to what it did? The government acted wholly and solely on the merits of the case, seeking to be perfectly fair and perfectly impartial, and the government advised this House of Commons in advance of what their full power of control over the situation would be. May I read the words? This was on February 25, 1929: Further with respect to the portion of the St. Lawrence which is wholly within Canada and indeed in respect to all navigable waters, this parliament is already secured in its powers of supervision under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, which gives to parliament the right not merely to review but to annul whatever may be done by the governor in council should it be shown that in any particular the action taken is unwise.
I ask hon. members to contemplate the significance of that statement at that time. That was not a statement made after there had been an investigation. That was not a statement made after approval had been given. That was a statement made a week or two in advance when this whole matter was being finally considered and the drafting of the clauses that were to protect the country and protect the rights of the people and the provinces were being most carefully considered and weighed. I continued:
Let me give to the house the sections of the Navigable Waters Protection Act "bearing on this question. Section 4 reads:
"No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site thereof has been approved by the governor in council nor unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council."
Section 10 provides:
"The governor in council may make such orders or regulations as he deems expedient for navigation purposes respecting any work to which this part applies or of which the plan and site are approved under any act of the parliament of Canada.
2. The local authority, company or person constructing, owning or in possession of any work shall be subject to such orders or regulations."	_
I come now to section 12, which is the important provision. This is the section which I wish hon. members to note particularly: "Parliament may, at any time, annul or vary any order of the governor in council made under this part."
Mr.' Adshead: Parliament?
Mr. Mackenzie King: Yes, parliament. Subsection 2 goes on:
"Any action of parliament in that behalf shall not be deemed an infringement of the rights of the local authority, company or person concerned."
Then I went on:
Where, then, is the need for adding anything to this particular act? rMr. Mackenzie King.]
That had reference to something that the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) had been discussing, I brought m the Beauharnois matter in that discussion. Someone asked me at the time, "Why did you bring the Beauharnois matter into something that has to do with natural resources?" That I believe was the question that was then under consideration. I replied that I was deliberately availing myself of 'my earliest opportunity to let hon. members know the exact position in regard to matters that were under consideration in the cabinet. I continued:
My hon. friend the member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) asked me the other day as to whether parliament would have the right to review certain matters which might be in contemplation. He has no need^ for concern as to the powers of parliament with respect to the possible acts of the government he had in mind whether they were of to-day or of six mopths ago or are still of the future; because parliament, with respect to the protection ot navigable matters under the act as it stands, has the power not only to review but to annul whatever may be done by the governor in council. Words cannot be stronger.	.
A little later I said:
I am merely seeking to make plain the points that bear particularly upon the St. Lawrence water development. I am not dealing with the other question. To that I have referred only incidentally. But this is very material to the question of the St. Lawrence development with respect to the rights of this parliament touching any act of the government by order in council or otherwise.
Mr. Garland (Bow River) [DOT] Would it not be better, sometimes not to pass an order in council than to have to annul it afterwards?
Mr. Mackenzie King: My hon. friend has asked a reasonable question, and I am glad that he has done so. There are some matters which are administrative in character, and others which are legislative; there are some questions which are technical and which can be dealt with only by experts, and other questions which are suitable for discussion in a deliberative assembly. When one comes to such questions as sites for water-power, the volume or rapidity of water passing over a particular point, the question of the effect of obstructions upon the levels of waters, the effect of the ice flow in certain localities, all of which are important questions when we are dealing with navigation, these questions can be settled, and settled only by expert engineers. They cannot be settled in a deliberative assembly. Most questions that relate to public works are of that character. They are questions for the experts of the government departments, and parliament in its wisdom has made clear that it is not advisable to prevent development by requiring in the first instance that parliament shall perform functions or duties which it is not at all fitted to perform. That is the reason this section is worded in the way it is. In other words, so far as provincial rights may be concerned, what :* sought by tile Navigable Waters Protection

Beauharnois Power-Report
Act is to allow the full development which provinces may seek with respect to power but where navigation is likely to be affected to assure at the same time that the general interest will be wholly and adequately secured.
That was on February 25. I am not going to weary the house much longer with citations, but I wish to give one more, and this is from what I said in the house two days later, on February 27, which bears on this matter. The citation is from the revised Hansard, page 525:	.
I think it is apparent that most of the problems respecting resources relate to the provinces. The provinces are primarily concerned with the natural resources, whether they be lands, mines, timber, waterpowers or other resources. I can conceive of nothing easier than to raise in this country the old issue of provincial rights if the federal government were to go beyond its jurisdiction and seek to perform in dealing with resources that belong to provinces acts which parliament never intended should be performed by a federal government. We have to be particularly careful in this Dominion, which is composed of provinces as well as a federal authority, to see that powers given to the Dominion for one purpose are not used to frustrate the rights of provinces as regards other matters which have been entrusted to them.
A good deal of discussion has taken ' place in connection with power resources, and I want to say a word in that connection, in order to make perfectly clear wherein the administration of water-powers within a province may belong to the province and not to the Dominion, and wherein there may be a difference of views as to powers generated in navigable waters. The question has arisen whether, under the rights which the Dominion has, with respect to the protection of navigable waters, the power that results from works constructed in a river for the purpose of improving navigation, would belong to the Dominion or the province. That question has been referred to the Supreme Court of Canada, and the answer that we have received, as I made clear the other day, is, to say the least, indecisive as to what, in that regard, are the rights of the respective parties
Some persons reading the judgment may say that the emphasis inclines in one direction, while others may say that it inclines in the other. I think the judges have indicated fairly clearly that they must have a concrete case before them before they will attempt to give any real decision as to the respective rights of the Dominion and the provinces. Wliat I wish at the moment to make clear is that, as regards navigable waters, the authority given to parliament to protect navigation and the means taken by parliament to exercise that authority enables the government, with respect to any applications that come before it for approval of plans of any company generating power in navigable waters, to impose such conditions as, in the opinion of its experts, are necessary to safeguard navigation. But it was never intended by any legislation of which I am aware, that the power which was given to the Dominion to protect navigation, was a power to be exercised to frustrate provinces
in the legitimate development of their own natural resources. That is an aspect of its rights and obligations which the government has to consider pretty carefully.
We have had placed before us by a company in the province of Quebec an application for the approval of certain plans that are essential in the development of power under a charter which lias given to that company by the province of Quebec. From much of the discussion in the public prints, one would think that the Dominion government was giving a charter for the right to develop water-power in the province of Quebec. The government has neither the power nor the authority to give a charter such as the one I refer to. The legislature of Quebec protects its own water-powers; that legislature gives its charters to companies in the light of its administration of its resources and what it may wish to have done with them, all that this government is called upon to do under the legislation which has been passed by parliament to protect navigable waters-navigable waters being a subject which by the British North America Act, is assigned to the Dominion parliament for protection and de-velopment

is to say whether or not those plans prejudice in any way or will injure the needs of navigation in the waters in which the works are to be placed or to which they may be related. When plans are submitted they do not go before a body of ministers; they go to expert engineers who examine them to see whether or not, they would be an obstruction to navigation, li they are, then the Dominion has no right to approve them. If they are not, the Dominion has then to consider whether there are other obligations of a general character of which account has to be taken? Where the river St. Lawrence is concerned, I submit there is a very real obligation of which the Dominion must take account: the Dominion, is obliged to see that any step which is taken under a provincial charter shall not be of a character which in any way will, in the first place, interfere with navigation, or, in the second place, prejudice [DOT]any possible scheme of development of navigation of which account ought to be taken because of the important national interests involved or to be considered. I ask this honourable house : Is there any relationship closer than that of father and son? He said he could not understand how a man could believe that governments were moved in that way. I agree with the minister in that. I say that any man who thinks that he can sway governments by the size of his contributions to political funds has not the first knowledge or understanding of human nature-perhaps I should say character-worthy of the name. What evidence is there on which to condemn an administration because of the fact that some man makes a very large contribution to a political campaign fund? All would depend upon what as a result was done. That company was undoubtedly looking for something in the way of consideration from governments. They are looking for something more from my right hon. friend to-day.
We provided in the order in council that if the company failed in any particular to do what was expected of them the government should always have the right to take over the whole concern. We have protected the public rights in every respect, where it appeared that the company might fall short in anything it was doing. Had we left out that consideration, had we not put in a clause in the order in council, with a view to safeguarding the government of the day, whatever might be its complexion, in the event of the company's failing to fulfil its obligations, then certainly we should have been at fault. I am sorry I have not the time to put on record all the safeguards that were

I am sorry to have taken as long as I have, but the reading of citations necessitated my doing so. I promise that I shall not be very long in concluding.
I have in my hand another order in council covering the appointment of a deputy minister. This order in council is da/ted December 11, 1924, which should be far enough removed from any Beauharnois relationship not to have any association with it. It reads as follows:
The committee of the privy council, on the recommendation of the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, the Prime Minister, advise that william Stuart Edwards, Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice, be appointed to be Deputy Minister of Justice vice Edmund Leslie New-eonibe, appointed judge of the Supreme Court of Canada.
When that appointment of Mr. Edwards was made, I made it on the advice of my colleague, the then Minister of Justice. He was the proper person to advise me whom he wished to have as his deputy, and I put forward the order.
I have here the order under which I appointed the successor to Mr. Henry, Mr. Valentine Irving Smart. Then here is an order'dated July 12, 1928, which reads:
The committee of the privy council, on the recommendation of the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, the Prime Minister, advise that Mr. William A. Found be appointed Deputy Minister of Fisheries under the authority of section 2, of chapter 62, of the statutes of 1926-27, at a salary-
And so forth. This was the regular way of proceeding. No one would say because I had appointed Mr. Found that there was something which necessitated the bringing of the name of the Prime Minister into the report of a select committee of the commons dealing with a
Beauhamois Power-Report

project such as the Beauharnois canal project. This kind of thing, I say, I believe would have been somewhat altered in any careful revision of the report.
May I say in regard to the appointment of Mr. Henry that it would be just as true to say that Major Graham Bell's death, which was the occasion of filling the vacancy of deputy minister was due to some circumstance connected with Beauhamois, as it would be to say that Mr. Henry was appointed because of any association with the Beauharnois interests? I ask hon. members to be reasonable in these matters. Consider the circumstances in which an administration is sometimes faced when very critical questions have to be dealt with. The late Mr. Graham Bell had a knowledge of Canadian railway conditions second to no other man in this country. There were very few who had any intimate knowledge of the railway business generally, of the work of the Department of Railways and Canals, and particularly of the work of the Canadian National Railways. When Mr. Graham Bell died, the Hon. Mr. Dunning, the then Minister of Railways and Canals, was at his wit's end to know where he could get a deputy minister who would be of any help to him wrhen the session come on.
It was a session during which a large program with respect to the Canadian National Railways was if possible to be put through parliament, and Mr. Dunning was filled with anxiety as to what he could do to fill that office so as to enable him to go on with that particular program. Mr. Henry had been for years in the Department of Railways and Canals, and was familiar with the general railway organization. He was at the time the economic expert on the Canadian National Railways, and as such knew about the Canadian National Railway system generally. The deputy minister had always been a member of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. He was the link between [DOT] the two. Mr. Henry helped to fill that particular role as no one else could possibly have filled it at the time it was necessary to fill the vacancy created by Major Bell's'death It was for that reason that Mr. Dunning sought to get the services of Mr. Henry.
Mr. Henry has given his own evidence. He has stated 'that he did not wish to accept the office, that he did not want it, but that Mr. Dunning pressed him and Sir Henry Thornton . pressed him in the railway interests. He says that he told Mr. Dunning that he was interested in Beauharnois. Mr. Dunning had [DOT] said to him: If Beauharnois was going to come before the Department of Railways and Canals in any shape or form he would not

allow him to come in, but that the Beauharnois application was before the Department of Public Works and that he would not be asked 'to have anything to do with the Beauhamois matter. The very day the evidence came out that Mr. Henry -was associated with the Sterling Industrial Corporation I asked Mr. Dunning whether that fact had been disclosed to him and whether he had had any knowledge of it, and he said to me that he had no knowledge of it whatsoever, that he did not know of the existence of the Sterling Industrial Corporation when he spoke to Mr. Henry, that until he read the evidence given before the commission he never had had any knowledge of its existence any more than I or, I imagine, any other members of the cabinet bad. If he had had the knowledge of what has since been disclosed, I am quite sure he would not have asked, pressing as the circumstances were, to have Mr. Henry fill the position for that time. Mr. Henry had to be persuaded against his own will and wish. He did what he did to oblige the government of the day and to render a much needed public service. He was at the time, as he said himself in giving his evidence, not in a condition physically where he felt he should take on extra burdens, and indeed he had to go into hospital for an operation very shortly after he took the appointment. All the circumstances, to anyone with an unbiased and free mind, make it perfectly clear that Mr. Henry's association with the Department of Railways and Canals was only because of the interests of this country, generously given with regard to its railway problems. It was for a temporary period only, until Mr. Dunning had had time to look around and obtain a successor. Mr. Dunning a little later was transferred to the Department of Finance, upon the death of Mr. Robb, which rendered necessary the keeping on of Mr. Henry for a little longer than would otherwise have been the case. He stayed only to oblige the administration in a critical situation.
Those are the facts. Why unless there is an ulterior political motive, this reference to Mr. Henry's appointment should be brought into the report in a way (to appear to reflect upon the head of the government of Canada, I am at a loss to understand. As I say, I would like 'to support this report in its entirety if it were not for things of this kind, buit when one encounters paragraphs of that sort one has to ask oneself: What view is the public going to take of the attitude of anyone who supports a report that contains that kind of insinuation and that kind of reflection?

May I say that the same kind of thing is true with respect to some other of the personal references in the report. Here I feel I come to tread on rather delicate ground. The report makes mention of several persons, some of whom are in pulblic life, some of whom are in the civil service, others of whom are citizens engaged in industrial and other concerns. I have always understobd with respect to this parliament that where matters concerned members of the other house it was for that house to concern itself with those particular individuals, that is was not for the members of this House of Commons to pass judgment upon any member of the honourable body of the Senate, any more than it is within the jurisdiction of the Senate to pass judgment upon an honourable member of this house. I do not want it to be assumed that I am trying to shield anyone, or to avoid any discussion, but I have the same; responsibility as the Prime Minister has in seeking to maintain the traditions of parliament, traditions that are fundamental, that are based on principle and that may operate in one way to-day as respects hon. members on this side and tomorrow may be operating in the same way as respects hon. members on the other side of the house. For that reason I say I was surprised when I found the report did refer in condemnatory terms to hon. members of the Senate. I would take no exception whatever to the committee taking all of the evidence that it wished to take, bringing it together in its report and making it as pointed. and direct and as strong as you please, and saying that this evidence should be submitted to the Senate of Canada-I am speaking now of the evidence that relates to the senators- for that honourable body to deal with. Indeed one of the recommendations of the report is that a copy of the report and 'the evidence shall be sent officially from this house to the Senate so that the Senate may take cognizance, of it. I submit that the Senate is the body that must deal with senators, and that we in this House of Commons have not the right to pass judgment on any member of the other house. I ask, Mr. Speaker, if I am not right in that view. Perhaps it is unnecessary to make an appeal offhand. I will leave it to the sense of the house. All that I want to make perfectly clear is this: I think a mistake is made in the report in presenting the matter in the way it is. Let me repeat, I would not have asked the committee to refrain from making a single statement about anything done by any senator that came out before the committee, but I do say that when they had brought out the, evidence, no matter how condemnatory in their opinion it
may have been, it was their duty where the evidence reflected upon honourable members of that body to recommend that the evidence be transmitted to the Senate for the Senate itself to deal with. Similarly in the House of Commons I believe we have here to maintain the rule and the tradition in that particular regard. If therefore I do not go into the question of any actions of the senators as referred to in the report it is because I am respecting what I believe to be the rules and the traditions of this parliament. Let me say most emphatically however that with respect to much set forth in the report concerning some of the things which have been- done, I believe they are wholly unjustifiable and cannot be defended a-t any cost. However with the matters contained in the report which pertain to senators it is for the Senate itself to deal.
There is one reference in the report, however to an honourable senator which I believe I should not allow to pass without comment, because it seems to cast a reflection on a hon. member of parliament which the evidence does not justify. I have before me that portion of the report which refers to Senator Raymond. It is to be found at page 638 of the votes and proceedings. Referring specially to subsection 2 of section 15, I quote the following:
At the conclusion of his evidence one of the members of tile committee expressed the view that he ought to be commended for his frankness in giving his evidence.
This is referring to Senator Raymond. Then, a little farther on I find the following:
It transpired when Mr. Sweezey returned to give further evidence that Senator Raymond had received from Mr. Sweezey some $200,000 of campaign funds for the Liberal party. The commendable frankness would seem to require that Senator Raymond should have disclosed this to the committee if he wished the committee to understand that he was stating fairly his connection between the government and the Beauharnois promoters.
I say that is not the evidence, and not even the inference to be drawn from the evidence. There are in those paragraphs insinuations and implications which under the circumstances are not at all justified. May I direct the attention of hon. members to the fact that Senator Raymond was never asked the question whether or not he received money for campaign funds. Senator Raymond offered to appear before the committee, came of his own volition, was present at the sittings and allowed members of the committee to examine him and ask any questions they wished. He answered every question. I am told that in fact he came back a second time.

May I say to the house that there were other witnesses who had appeared before the committee and had been questioned, but to whom no questions were put concerning campaign funds. Mr. Sweezey himself had been on the stand more than one day. At a later time he was recalled and asked concerning campaign funds, but this was at a time subsequent to that at which Senator Raymond had given his evidence. When Senator Raymond gave his evidence the matter of campaign funds had not been discussed in the committee. Under those circumstances I ask:	Was it
fair for a committee wishing to be perfectly impartial and judicial to inject this reference into the report:
At the conclusion of his evidence one of the members of the committee expressed the view that he ought to be commended for his frankness in giving his evidence.
There was no need to insert that sentence in the report. It was put in to form an excuse for inserting the following paragraph:
It transpired when Mr. Sweezey returned to give further evidence

Those are the words, "when Mr. Sweezey returned to give further evidence." Why was that evidence not brought out at the lreginning? Hon. members in the committee had knowledge during the several meetings of the facts that they were going to bring out with respect to campaign funds, and with respect to everything else. They had that knowledge before the committee ever met. Why did' they not ask Mr. Sweezey about campaign funds when he was questioned at the start?

I say that Senator Raymond was perfectly frank when he appeared before the committee. He answered all questions asked him and he was never asked any question about campaign funds. The evidence does not disclose anything which would afford reason for an attitude of that kind.
I should like now to pass on to further matters. I do not wish to take up too much time in a discussion of individual names, but reference has been made to two civil servants and in that connection I think I should speak briefly. The report contains a reference to Mr. J. B. Hunter, Deputy Minister of Public Works, and to Mr. K. M. Cameron, chief engineer of that department. True, the report does not say very much about these gentlemen, but refers to the manner in which they gave their evidence. I feel the statement ought to be made that at all times, civil servants are in a very difficult position. They are in the public service under the direction of ministers, but they are not in positions where they can speak for themselves. A reflection may be cast, in a report such as this, upon two members of the public service,

Beauharnois Power-Report
and yet they are not at liberty to so much as come out in the press the next day and make an explanation of their conduct.
I gather that in the committee there was a good deal of questioning of witnesses and it may have been that there was something in the manner of these gentlemen that was not altogether pleasing to members of the committee. But let anyone go through the ordeal of appearing before a parliamentary committee to give evidence, and I should be rather surprised if his manner would be all that one might expect from a person expert in the matter of giving evidence. In this case I submit if these gentlemen gave their evidence in a manner which was not satisfactory the whole purpose would have been served had the minister in charge, the chairman of the committee, spoken to his colleague, the Minister of Public Works, about the manner in which the evidence was being given, and requested the Minister of Public Works to speak to those particular civil servants concerning the manner in which their evidence had been given. That would I believe have been a fair way to deal with public servants, but I do not think it is fair that the names of these two very worthy men who have been in the service of Canada for a long time and who have given excellent service, should be broadcast across Canada, coupled with the kind of thing contained in this report, thereby carrying the inference that in some way they too were connected with what there may be in the way of scandal revealed therein.

That is another reason why I should hesitate to approve fully of the report in its present form, strongly as I am prepared to endorse most of what it contains.
That concludes about all I wish to say at the moment with respect to individuals whose names are mentioned. I come now to the concluding portion of my remarks which deal with the matter of political organization and campaign funds. At this point I shall ask hon. members to allow me to review the situation, as did the Minister of Immigration, in its true perspective. I wish to state my own position as head of the party I have the honour to lead, and from the standpoint of my relation to the whole question of political organization.
I was chosen leader of the Liberal party at the national convention in 1919-chosen by the votes of the majority present at the convention, which happily included a majority
of the then members of the Liberal party in the House of Commons. On some previous occasions leaders have been chosen only from the parliamentary group. My right hon. friend was chosen at a great convention of his party. I think he is the first leader of his party who has been chosen in that way. I mention this matter simply because it has some bearing upon the question of the organization of a political party. The proceedings of that convention have been published, and are available to all hon. members of this house. In the proceedings are given the twofold purpose of the convention: (1) to choose a leader; (2) to arrange for party organization. Page 12 reads as follows:
In the official call for the national Liberal convention it is stated that the second purpose for which the convention is to be held will be to deal with the question of party organization. The importance of party organization was, therefore, present to the minds of those who prepared the official call, and it should not occupy a lesser place in the minds of those who may be given an opportunity to deal with the subject either as members of a committee or in the convention as a whole.
The convention took up the question of party organization, and it was decided that there should be a national committee of which the leader of the party would be the president or honorary president, there were to be vicepresidents from the different provinces, and a committee of fifty odd in number. There was to be a national Liberal organization office to be established in the city of Ottawa, which would have charge of organization and information. Mr. Haydon had been secretary of the national convention. He generously consented to act as secretary of this office. Probably I am wrong in saying he acted as secretary; I think he was to be general counsel, although he assumed in large part the obligations of secretary. That was in 1919. The work of carrying on such publicity as was issued on behal" of the party was centred in this office, and when political campaigns came on those who were associated with the office had to do with those campaigns.
There were by-elections prior to the general election of 1921. With regard to those byelections, as leader of the party I had no knowledge whatsoever of the organization of the campaigns, I did not regard it as part of my duty as leader of the party to have to do with the work of organizing political campaigns. I could never have hoped to fill the position of leader of my party in this house had I, in addition to the duties of preparing for the subjects of debate here and the obligation of speaking publicly throughout the country, to take charge of political campaigns

Beauharnois Power-Report

I simply could not have done it even if it had been expected of me as a political leader, which it was not. I had nothing to do with the organization of the by-elections prior to 1921. When the general election of 1921 came on, I had no knowledge whatever of how that campaign was managed-I went where I was told to go to speak by those who had direction of the campaign. I had just about all I could do to get together the material that was needed for speaking in that campaign from one end of the country to the other.
How could I, as leader of the Liberal party at that time, having had very little experience in public life, have taken charge of such organization work? I was returned to parliament in 1908, and during the greater part of that year I was in the orient. When I arrived back in Ottawa before the end of the session the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier honoured me by taking me into his cabinet, and I continued as Minister of Labour until 1911. I was busy with my departmental work during that time and was not dealing with questions of political organization. While I was out of parliament after 1911, I had for a time to do with some of the publicity work of the party, writing pamphlets, and also editing the Liberal monthly publication. But during the time I held the position no election campaigns took place, and I had no knowledge of the organization of political campaigns. When I came back into parliament in 1919, I had had very little in the way of political experience. With such ability as I had it required just about all the time and resource I could command to master the questions that presented themselves for debate and discussion without attempting in addition to deal with election campaigns. So during the campaign qf 1921 I had no knowledge whatever of who contributed to the campaign funds or how the campaign was conducted.
Now, what was true of the by-elections prior to 1921 was equally true of all by-elections which took place subsequent to 1921; what was true of the general election of 1921 was equally time of the general election of 1925, the general election of 1926 and the general election of 1930-the position was exactly the same. With respect to the political organization of the party or the knowledge of its affairs in 1930 my attitude was no different from that which it had been in previous years. There was no reason why it should be. I held to the position which I hold to at this moment, and which I say is the only true position that a political leader can take-that
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
there must be a division of labour in a political party, that it is the duty of the political head of the party to see to matters of policy, to be able to discuss questions on the floor of parliament and throughout the country; but that it is not his business to get out the literature of the party, nor is it his business to organize political campaigns. Such work belongs to the rank and file of the party and to those who will act on their behalf.
In that particular may I say that I believe I am following the tradition which has always been followed in British politics. Will anyone say-I will not speak of those who are in active politics to-day, and I will not speak of those who have been politically active in this country, but I will speak of some of the great political leaders in Great Britain who have passed away. Will anyone say that Mr. Gladstone had supervision of the organization of the Liberal party and its campaigns in England during the time he was Prime Minister and leader of the party?

speechtext:
Yes, and I
am glad my right hon. friend has spoken of that. I will have a word to say in that regard, because it brings out the essential difference between our points of view. In England the organization of the Liberal party was a development of the national federation. Its secretary was Mr. Robert Hudson, a gentleman who subsequently became Sir Robert Hudson. For a third of a century he was secretary of the national Liberal federation, an organization of the party as a whole whose affairs were controlled by representatives of the party from all parts of England. He was also secretary of another special council which had to do with political matters, the Liberal Central Association. This national federation carried on the work of the Liberal party throughout the country and in the constituencies; it had to do with the sending out of literature, the placing of speakers and the organizing of political campaigns. In parliament the whips of the party had their own organization in association with the Prime Minister, but that organization had nothing to do with political campaigns. The whole work of political campaigning, as I have said, was kept separate and distinct from the Prime Minister and his associates; they may have been in touch with it but it would have been impossible for any prime minister to attempt to grasp all the details.
I do not ask hon. members to accept my word* for this. I hold in my hand a volume which is a memoir of Sir Robert Hudson, published by Mr. J. A. Spender, who for many years was editor of the Westminster Gazette and who is well known as the distinguished author amongst many other works of the Life and Times of Campbell-Bannerman and other volumes entitled "The Public Life." This memoir of Sir Robert Hudson contains a statement of the organization of the Liberal party in England over a period of forty
years. If hon. members wish to know about the organizer and his work they will find in chapter 3 a full account of how the organizing is carried on, under the following headings:
Appointment as secretary to the N.L.F.; A dual office; The Liberal central association and its functions; A working partnership; Robert's friendships and their value; The duties of the secretary; Visitors to the office; Supplying candidates; Arranging public meetings; Difficulties with the star performers; Providing "literature;" The Liberal publication department; The Liberal magazine.
That chapter contains a complete statement of the organizer and his work in connection with the Liberal party in England. Then there is another chapter which goes even more fully into the matter we are now considering. It has to do with the Liberal party and its finances. This subject is discussed under the following headings:
Asquith at Dean's Yard; Work at Abingdon
Street; Anxiety and hope; The financial storm-centre; The 1923 election; The Lloyd George fund; Negotiations with Mr. Lloyd George; The disaster of 1924; The million fund; Its difficulties; The general strike and Lord Oxfords resignation; Renewed negotiations with ,r* iloy!l George; Their outcome; Resignation of officers.
This chapter makes clear that the split in the Liberal party of England, which is more or less irretrievable, was the result of the introduction into Liberal politics of a plan of organization by one of the political heads of that party which had never existed previously. Mr. Lloyd George, who had been head of the Union government, acquired control of a campaign fund which, as is generally known, was largely derived from the sale of titles. They get their campaign funds in one way or another in the old country as well as in this country. Over there they got them larglely from the sale of titles, and when Mr. Lloyd George had this fund he earned it with him away from his position as head of the Union government to his position as leader of the Liberal party. The Liberals who were of the old school, and who believed in the party itself looking after its own organization, were not satisfied with that sort of dictatorship. It shocked their sense of independence, they felt that it gave a political leader who had all the power in his own hands, the right to dictate policies, to control constituencies and to make conditions in a dozen and one ways with respect to the general business of the party. They thought no political leader should have any such power, at least in the Liberal party, so they

Beauharnois Power-Report
decided to issue a call asking the Liberals of England to subscribe to a million pound fund.
What was the result of that call? The Liberals of England asked, "What about this fund Mr. Lloyd George has? They said: We do not intend to subscribe a million pounds while the party has a fund as large as that in the possession of Mr. Lloyd George." The leaders of the party could not very well explain that Mr. Lloyd George was attaching all sorts of conditions to the use of that fund, and through their inability to give any explanation of the kind they were unable to gather in subscriptions to any appreciable amount. The result has been that large numbers of Liberals have left Mr. Lloyd George altogether simply because they do not wish to have at the head of their party anyone who has complete control of the party purse.

The view I hold is that with respect to any funds relating to campaign purposes it is not 'the duty of the leader of the political party to have to do with these matters. It is for the party organization formed expressly for the purpose by the party itself.
Now may I go a step further. This memoir of Sir Robert Hudson contain appreciations of the work done by the secretary of the Liberal organization, and I want to read a few words from these appreciations because they confirm what I have all along held to be the relationship between the secretary of the national organization and Whoever might hold .the office of Prime Minister or leader of the party. I quote from page 187:
In his dual capacity of secretary of the national Liberal federation and secretary of the Liberal central association, Robert at the time of his death had had a longer continuous association with the intimate affairs of a great political party than any man then living. His service stretched back to the days when Mr. Gladstone was in the plenitude of his power, and Mr. Chamberlain the enthusiastic leader of the Radical left-wing; he was appointed to the highest place in the administration of the Liberal party when Mr. Gladstone was still on the scene, and remained at his post for thirty-three years in intimate relations with three prime ministers and a succession of leaders and whips, by all of whom he was trusted and respected. Though he died in the prime of life, the years in which he lived were crowded with events of overwhelming importance, and he had an inner vision of them and of the chief actors in them vouchsafed to very few- men of his generation.
There is a true picture of one who hold's the office of chief organizer of a political party formed on the lines I have indicated. Here is a further word that throws a little light on the relations of an organizer to his party:
So far as Robert was concerned, life behind the scenes was one of cheerful and loyal com-

It would be strange indeed if Senator Haydon had not been a close personal friend of my own. He was a close personal friend and is a close personal friend of mine; he was a friend throughout the years that he held the position of secretary of the national office and before that time. And may I say that if I were asked to describe the relationship between us, as I have believed it to be all the time, I would do so in the words which are used here by Mr. Spender in reference to the one who held the office of chief organizer of the Liberal party in Britain. What else is said in this volume by way of appreciation of this man who was chief organizer of his party?
The confidence that Hudson at once inspired in men, even rich men, wary of their pockets, was extraordinary. Rich men would give him thousands when they would not have given prime ministers a penny piece, and yet Hudson had nothing to offer them in return save his good-will, for the federation possessed neither patronage nor power, and never attempted, or would have been allowed, to interfere with the arrangements of the whips' room.
That is the position in England. The chief organizer of the party had to do with the obtaining of party funds and he obtained them from different persons. Mr. Spender, who has perhaps a more intimate knowledge of the politics of Great Britain than any other living man, certainly than any other Liberal in Great Britain, says that there were men who gave the chief organizer thousands when they would not have given a prime minister a cent. And yet so scrupulously careful were they in Britain, or have -been so far as I can judge, to prevent political leaders from being placed in a position of embarrassment through knowledge of what contributions may be made to party funds, that, as the writer says here, the organizer-

That is the position; and I cannot make it too clear that, so far as the Prime Minister and his colleagues in the late administration were concerned, they were attending to the business of government, attending to their duties as ministers of the crown, and were not concerning themselves with the question of raising party funds or of working out party campaigns. They may have assisted. But the fact that contributions were made to a party campaign fund, no matter what their amount, cannot possibly carry with it, except to those who are inclined to think in that way, the inference that these funds were going to influence at any time either the present or any future action of the administration of the day.
I was struck, in reading this book, with a remark about the way Sir Robert Hudson felt in regard to this obnoxious and thankless business of collecting political campaign funds, and obtaining moneys wherewith to run the organization. It discloses how difficult it is in England or elsewhere to obtain funds. Here is a paragraph which appears at page 174:

May I say to my right hon. friend that I have stated quite frankly my point of view as to the organization of political campaigns and the duty of a leader with respect to political campaign funds. I hold the view I do for two reasons. The first one is the one which I have already given, namely, that it would be humanly impossible for me as the -leader of the Liberal party to attempt to do my duty in this House of Commons and deal with the questions which are before us if I were to be continually harassed through having to do with questions of party organization and political campaigns. I could not have done it in the past, I cannot do it now, and I will not do it in the future. Unless the party of which I am the head can find some means of having the work of publicity and organization carried on without my being responsible for it, and for the organization of political campaigns then all I can say is that they will have to find someone else to lead the party. It would be an impossible task for any man who is in this particular position and I have always so indicated to members of the party ever since I have been its leader.
But I have another reason. I think I have some faith in my own integrity and in my purpose in public life. I would not care to have to deal with the questions with which this house has to deal and be possessed of an inventory of those who had contributed to the party funds. I would not care to know who the men were or what the amounts were which they had given for purposes of political campaigns. I want to make a distinction with respect to the issuing of literature and for the work of the Liberal information office from month to month and from year to year. I have time and again asked leading members of the party if they would not make some small contribution in order to help out with our literature, and a very few friends of the party have been generous in that regard. I felt that that was a perfectly legitimate thing to do. These names and amounts can be made public at any time; these contributions have been made in order to help the party publish what literature it has been in a position to get out. All the time that I have been the leader of the party I have never asked a single individual to make a contribution to a political campaign. I have had no knowledge of what the political campaign funds were. As I have said, I cannot see how a political leader could have in his pocket an inventory of the contributions made by those who have

I say that the view that I take of a prime minister's obligation is that it is not part of his duty, and it must not be expected of him, to know what contributions have been made to political campaign funds. I may be wrong in that, but that is the position I take.
May I add this? I do not see how anyone could possibly be expected to know what contributions are being made to party funds. After all, is the Prime Minister going to* be told everything? Some things come from one source, others from another source, some in direct ways, others in indirect ways. How can he possibly know? I think any doctrine that the Prime Minister should know is as unfair to those who make political contributions as to those who ask for them. Many a man might wish to contribute to his party and the policies it advocates, but if he knew that the leader was going to know what his contribution was he might hesitate to make a contribution, feeling that it would be embarrassing both to him and to the head of the government. In the Ottawa Journal of Thursday, July 23, 1931, there is an article W'hich is headed, "Mr. Mackenzie King and Beauhamois." The first part of that article has reference to my own personal honour as leader of the opposition. I should like to thank the Ottawa Journal for w'hat it has said in regard to myself personally, as I do thank as well other publications both on the Conservative and the Liberal side which have been generous enough to say a word at this time with respect to what they believed to be the personal honour of one who has held the office of Prime Minister in this country for nearly ten years. The article in this particular reads:
In the matter of campaign funds, and in the particular matter of that $700,000 which Mr. Sv'eezey handed over to Senators Haydon and Raymond, Mr. King's position is not so happy. Here, we think, the country will want to know' the answer to those questions:

My answer to that is that I do not know. Senator Haydon was known to be and had been known to be for years the organizer and treasurer of the party, so far as Ottawa and the general work w'as concerned. I assume that he would naturally be thought of as the one to whom contributions should be made. As hon. members well know, in political campaigns a great many are only too anxious to be the collectors of political funds, and I think it is fortunate for a political party when it is known that only one or two men have the right to receive contributions. The province of Quebec, so far as the Liberal party is concerned, whether it relates to the Dominion or the province, has always preferred to manage its own affairs, and in that province Senator Raymond acted as treasurer for the party- a very difficult task, a very obnoxious task in many ways, but assumed by him as his share of the party's work in a political campaign, and generously assumed.

May I just say a further word in regard to this matter? Some of the papers of the country have been saying that the Liberal party has been brought into disgrace by what has taken place. After all, it is an unfortunate fact with regard to most things in human life, that no matter how good the cause may be, no matter how true and honourable and honest the great body of men and women are who are supporting a cause, every now and then something happens which is not creditable, and the party as a whole or the group as a whole have to suffer as a consequence. During the period of the great war when men were fighting for liberty and giving their lives for the cause, things happened to the commissariat which were most discreditable. There were scandals in connection with the food that was supplied, in connection with the boots and shoes supplied, even in connection with the munitions supplied, scandals which everyone deplored, and I am sure no one more than those who belonged to the great army in the fighting forces. But will anyone say that because some of the army organization or those connected with it did things that were not creditable, that their actions brought the whole army into disgrace or that the great cause for which
they were fighting had suffered thereby. No one could deplore more than I do what has been revealed in this inquiry. I am glad if it was there to bring out, that everything has come out that has come out. I would much rather have everything known than that anything should be concealed with no end of rumours and suspicions continually afloat. What I want to say is this. Individual members of the Liberal party may have done what they should not have done, But the whole party is not thereby disgraced. The party is not disgraced, but it is in the valley of humiliation. I tell the people of this country today that as its leader I feel humiliated, and I know my following feel humiliated. I have told them so in caucus, that we are in the valley of humiliation. But we are going to come out of that valley, not in any boasting way, but with a determination to see to it that so far as the cause of Liberalism in this country is concerned, it will advance forward to higher and stronger and better ground than it has ever occupied in the past.

If it is not done, the country will increasingly come to the conclusion that the purpose of the select committee has been not so much to gain information concerning the Beauharnois canal project as to bring out certain facts known in advance concerning what has been done by one or two members of the Liberal party in order that the Conservative party might be shielded with respect to what it has done in political campaigns.

I am not making any charges, but I think the country will be interested in knowing how large contributions have been, what individual contributions have been, what every member who has contributed to the party has given. After all, it is not merely the fact that individuals contribute but the amounts which are given which are of importance during election times. A contribution of half a million dollars-

May I add that I believe it is a great mistake that the -public should have the idea that because campaign funds are large, and large amounts are contributed, that they are used for the purposes of corrupting the electorate or for buying votes. I do not believe of late campaign funds have been used in that way by any of the political parties in this -country.

We would be in a position to find those things out for ourselves if my right hon. friend would grant the commission I -am now asking for in the name of the country.
I think that not only should there be a royal commission to go into the matter of party campaign funds from the ground up, so that if at all possible we may have the

The Governor General
matter cleared up once and for all, but as soon as the next session of parliament meets there should be appointed a select committee of the house to consider the Dominion Elections Act, and see if in some way it is not possible to have that act further amended so as to render unnecessary, to as large a degree as possible, the collection of moneys for campaign purposes. I make that suggestion in the interests of every hon. member in the house, in the interest of every future candidate, in the interests of every political party, and in the public interest. I would suggest the establishment of a permanent register which would record the name of every elector who is entitled to vote, such register to be kept up to date by the chief electoral officer so that when there is a by-election or a general election no money will have to be spent to make out voters' lists, or for other like purposes. May I add that when in office we considered the register idea, and had time permitted would have put it into force. I had consulted with Colonel Biggar, who had to do with the drafting of the elections act some years ago and he told me that two years at least would be required to put such legislation into effect. There was not time before the general election to bring it into effect, but the government now in office might have time to deal with the matter.
In addition to the suggestions I have made there should be a measure to make it the law of the land that voting shall be compulsory. Under such a law every voter would be expected to go to the polls and record his vote, whether he marked his ballot for one party or for another, or simply sent it in in blank. It is the duty of every one to vote, a first duty of citizenship; and if the last two measures I have mentioned were put into effect I believe they would go a long way towards putting an end to the necessity of campaign funds and everything associated with them. In the third place, if any way can be found of limiting the amounts of subscriptions to be given by individuals, companies or corporations, and any way of giving increased publicity to whatever is given, I believe such measures would be very much in the public interest.
It would be a grave mistake, after the inquiry has gone so far, if the matter were allowed to rest as it now stands. The public conscience in Canada has been aroused, and we should take advantage of that fact to see that as much information and as much light as possible is thrown on the whole matter of party organization and campaign funds, and that legislation be enacted to ensure at election time hereafter as little necessity as possible for campaign funds. If we do that, then possibly some great good will come of the inquiry which has been held, and which has been such a heartbreak to many of us on this side of the house.
